subject: A new study suggests HIV prevention has stalled. But there may be a silver lining
posts:
New cohort data reveals South Africa's HIV prevention progress has stalled since 2019, even as youth infection rates drop. 🌐
Evidence: Stalled Overall Progress, Youth Infection Drop, Rigorous District Cohort Data
#SouthAfrica #PublicHealth

Spotlight and GroundUp report that a major Lancet HIV study in KwaZulu-Natal shows HIV prevention plateauing since 2019, though youth infections continue falling, calling for expanded national studies.
Stated Judgement: (+0.68, +0.50) — Greater Good

Ground truth confirms the study uses robust 20-year cohort data from uMkhanyakude. COVID disruptions and PEPFAR aid cuts created real headwinds, but youth declines offer a silver lining needing state focus.
Resulting Judgement: (+0.53, +0.35) — Greater Good

Verdict: PASS — Small Fall from Grace.
Integrity: Absolute Truth (Hypocrisy: 0.05, z: 0)

- GroundUp / Spotlight: PASS (+0.85, +0.80) — Honest, nuanced public health reporting.
- SA Dept of Health: COND (+0.20, -0.10) — Treatment stalled; needs expanded research.

A 20-year cohort study in KZN published in The Lancet HIV shows that overall HIV incidence plateaued after 2019. Despite funding cuts and COVID-19 disruptions, infection rates among young adults aged 15-24 continued to decline.

The Bright Side:
Despite macro funding disruptions from US PEPFAR cuts and pandemic challenges, targeted prevention efforts among younger demographics are working, demonstrating that focused intervention can curb transmission.

Plane Error (Physical Q3 vs Possible Q2): Critics risk confusing localized district trend lines with nationwide failure. The authors explicitly avoid over-generalizing, correctly distinguishing localized empirical sampling from broader national policy assumptions.

Social Physics Analysis:
GroundUp executes a Smart Altruistic maneuver by presenting complex, mixed public health findings with complete transparency. Rather than sensationalizing stalled progress or ignoring aid cuts, they empower readers with rigorous, nuanced evidence.

The Trajectory: The Path of Small Fall from Grace.
Modal Dynamics: May be -> is like via Green Bottom (Empirical Anchor). Grounded cohort data validates progress in youth while establishing empirical anchors for national public health strategy.

The Unavoidable Truth: Localized long-term cohort tracking provides the reliable empirical foundation needed for honest public health strategy.

The Unavoidable Lie: Single-district plateaus do not prove nationwide policy failure.

Alethekanon:
Empirical rigor demands holding complex truths simultaneously. Declining youth incidence proves interventions work, while overall plateaus highlight the systemic danger of foreign aid shocks.

Spirithekanon:
"Test everything; hold fast to what is good." 1 Thessalonians 5:21 — PASS
Rigorous empirical examination reveals hidden progress amid broader setbacks, guiding wise action.

Stated Claim / Post Context:
A new study suggests HIV prevention has stalled. But there may be a silver lining

Infections dropped sharply in the 2010s, but progress since 2019 is unclear. More studies are needed across the country

Actual Article Body:
Three-dimensional images of HIV superimposed on electron micrographs of the virus. Constructed by Stephen Fuller, Centre for Human Genetics, Oxford University and taken from front cover of Equal Treatment March 2006.

The two key goals in managing the HIV epidemic are getting as many people with the virus as possible onto ARV treatment and reducing the number of new infections. The results of a study from KZN, published in The Lancet HIV, suggest we’re stalling on the prevention front. The study is well done and important, but the situation may not be as bleak as the authors suggest.

Following the abrupt cuts in United States aid last year, many feared that South Africa’s HIV treatment and prevention efforts would suffer. Though early signs are that the worst-case scenario hasn’t unfolded, figures published in May this year did indicate that South Africa’s ARV treatment programme stalled in 2025.

Now a major new study published by Elphas Okango and his colleagues in The Lancet HIV suggests that the country’s HIV response may have been losing steam even before the aid cuts. But the study took place in one district, uMkhanyakude in KwaZulu-Natal (KZN), so one should be cautious about generalising to the whole country. The authors found a large reduction in new infections in the mid-2010s, but the picture from 2019 onward is less clear.

From 2013 to 2018, the researchers estimate that HIV incidence (the rate of new HIV infections) declined by 52% in males and 37% in females. After that, HIV incidence plateaued from 2019 to 2025 in both men and women, according to the authors. One interesting nuance in the data is that HIV incidence continued to decline among young adults, but this was offset by increasing incidence in older adults. Moreover, the number of people with detectable HIV viraemia increased from 2019 to 2025 by 10%.

The researchers estimate the lifetime risk of people in the study population becoming HIV-positive at about one in two for women and three in ten for men.

While the new data is from only one district, the nature of the data is particularly well suited for calculating HIV incidence. That is because it is cohort data. In short, researchers from the Africa Health Research Institute (AHRI) have been testing largely the same tens of thousands of people in the same communities for HIV every year from 2003 to 2025. This means they could observe when people’s test results went from negative to positive. There are other methods for estimating HIV incidence, but this is one of the most reliable.

The researchers suggest several factors may have contributed to the loss of momentum.

First, they say that early gains during the scale-up of antiretroviral treatment may have already been made and that further declines will be “increasingly difficult to sustain as ongoing transmission becomes concentrated in harder-to-reach groups”.

Second, they suggest that the ageing of the HIV epidemic has shifted the burden of new infections towards increasingly older adults, who might be less likely to perceive themselves as being at risk and remain underserved by existing prevention programmes.

And finally, “behavioural changes, including declines in condom distribution reported in some settings, might also have contributed by making earlier reductions in transmission more difficult to sustain”.

The study appears to be well conducted and the authors’ analysis is sound. But are the authors’ conclusions too pessimistic? Possibly.

It could be that, for reasons beyond the authors control, the data are too messy to capture what progress there may have been. Covid disrupted so much of South African life, and is likely one reason why the data is a bit chaotic after 2019.

Incidence in this population declined in 2019. There was a disruption in 2020 and 2021 due to covid and so no incidence is given. The decline continued in 2022, then rose in 2023, declined again in 2024 and then reached its lowest ever level in 2025. While the numbers from 2019 to 2025 are a bit all over the place and the decline isn’t statistically significant (and consequently may be due to random fluctuations), it could still be real.

Even so, there is no obvious explanation as to why the percentage of people with detectable viraemia has increased in this population. We also don’t know whether the same thing is happening in other parts of the country. All of this is concerning.

To better understand what is going on, South Africa needs more such HIV incidence studies in several more districts spread across multiple provinces. The Minister of Health together with the Department of Health and the Department of Science, Technology and Innovation can show leadership by making that happen.

Low is the editor of Spotlight. Geffen is the director of GroundUp.
